newsitem.title: USA: Clinton faces foreign policy challenges.
newsitem.headline: Clinton faces foreign policy challenges.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, having clinched re-election, must come to grips quickly with some major foreign policy challenges.
They include whether to keep U.S. troops in Bosnia and how to deal with growing Russian resistance to NATO enlargement.
Clinton had delayed decisions on controversial foreign policy issues so they would not become a distraction -- or a detriment -- in the 1996 presidential campaign.
But with the election now over, he must confront these straight on, as well as the expected appointment of a replacement for Secretary of State Warren Christopher.
Defence Secretary William Perry is likely to stay on in the new administration, which begins Jan. 20, at least for a while, U.S. officials say.

A NATO study on options for Bosnia once an alliance-led implementation force (IFOR) departs early next year is supposed to be released on Wednesday. U.S. officials told Reuters that Clinton will have about two weeks to decide if American troops will be part of an expected IFOR follow-on force.

Clinton initially vowed the 20,000 U.S. troops sent to Bosnia would be out by the end of 1996. Other officials perpetuated that idea, even as it became increasingly apparent some kind of international force had to remain in that troubled country.
Many experts believe Clinton has little choice but to join the follow-on force, given the central U.S. role in the Bosnia peace process.

The administration was also holding its breath most of this presidential election year about Russia. It hoped growing political instability intensified by President Boris Yeltsin's health problems would not trigger a crisis that could hurt Clinton, who claimed U.S. policy toward Russia a success.
Yeltsin had his heart bypass operation on Tuesday and was reported doing well. But it will be some time before he recovers enough to assume full duties.

The power vacuum in Moscow for at least the last six months has been accompanied by a troubling "toughening" of Russia's attitude toward Clinton's campaign to expand NATO into eastern Europe, senior officials told Reuters.
With NATO moving steadily toward taking on new members, "that is the biggest issue in the U.S.-Russia relationship ... The problem is the foreign ministry," one official said.

Other major issues must be dealt with in the next month. Christopher heads for the Middle East next week, where officials hope there will soon be a long-delayed Israel-Palestinian peace agreement on Hebron.

Beyond that, "you will ... after some period of reflection, see an intensification of the effort to bring peace to the Middle East," but chances of a comprehensive deal are low, one official said. U.S. negotiator Dennis Ross is well-regarded by the Clinton team and will not be asked to leave his post.

Christopher is also set to visit China Nov. 19-21 in an effort to keep that thorny but critical relationship on a stable track. Clinton then meets Chinese President Jiang Zemin in Manila on the fringes of a regional economic meeting.
Clinton has not laid out a comprehensive foreign policy strategy for his next term. But recent speeches and interviews with senior officials give some idea of what can be expected.

With foreign policy spending down 51 percent since 1984, the State Department faces a funding crisis and officials say Clinton will make that an early priority. But Congress is still dominated by opposition Republicans, leading advocates of such spending cuts, and reversing that trend will be hard.
Clinton made only passing reference to foreign policy in his victory speech, stressing the need to "work together" and "put country ahead of party."

Officials say he will have to spend time improving strained ties with European allies, and they expect he will find a way to sidestep a provision involving lawsuits in the anti-Cuba Helms-Burton law that outraged those allies.
The officials see no early change in the dual-containment policy toward Iran and Iraq, but do not rule out a review once a new secretary of state takes office.
U.S. efforts to advance democracy in Haiti and maintain a nuclear freeze pact with North Korea also must be tended, as well as strained relations with Turkey, a key NATO ally.

Christopher met Clinton on Tuesday and may soon announce plans to resign, but is expected to stay in office at least until January. U.N. Ambassador Madeleine Albright and former Senate Majority Leader George Mitchell are considered leading candidates to succeed him. Some say Mitchell has an edge after helping Clinton prepare for the election debates.
Insiders do not rule out former Bosnia peacemaker Richard Holbrooke, Democratic Sen. Sam Nunn of Georgia or some Republican who could help negotiate with Congress on Clinton's foreign policy agenda.
